limitations: This is a curated behavior denominator grounded in the public_headers list in common/meson.build and public API gtk-doc comments for those declarations. It is not an exhaustive specification or a mechanical function inventory. Private functions, even those with gtk-doc comments, are not public API requirements.

Each requirement needs assertions of its described outcome. Calling a function, using a getter as an argument, printing a value, or connecting and logging a signal does not establish the contract. The surfaces list identifies directly required API outcomes, not setup dependencies or a scenario coverage mapping.

Requirements with profile any describe profile-independent contracts or contracts applicable to either installation profile. They do not imply that both profiles were tested. Explicit system requirements remain in the denominator even when the environment cannot provision system services, authorization, additional installations, or multiple users.

Ownership examples and argument permutations are not exhaustive. NULL versus empty arrays, flags and flag combinations, architectures, branches, locales, malformed inputs, error paths, concurrency, and cancellation timing need further cases. These requirements impose no ABI, binary-layout, symbol-version, or introspection-compatibility requirement.

Deprecated direct installation APIs remain public and have distinct contracts. In particular, a no-op direct update documents ALREADY_INSTALLED, whereas a transaction can successfully contain no non-skipped update operations. Coverage of the transaction API does not cover the deprecated entry points.

The existing blackbox client launches applications through the CLI driver. Such execution is useful corroborating evidence for installed state but earns no libflatpak launch, instance, or run coverage. Launch and instance obligations below require separate public library assertions.

Public documentation does not promise database-style rollback of a whole transaction. It promises atomic individual operations and retention of already completed operations after a later failure. Failure-preservation requirements use fixtures whose other refs have no pending changes.

FlatpakError documents ABORTED as resulting from TRUE in operation-error, but the public operation-error signal documentation says TRUE continues and FALSE stops. The signal-specific contract is used below; the contradictory enum prose is not used to require an exact outer error code. A failing operation's GError and the transaction's outer GError must not be conflated.

flatpak_transaction_run prose says operation-error is emitted for an error at any point, while the section and signal documentation describe executed operations. Signal sequencing requirements below concern executed operations and do not require an operation-error signal for every resolution failure. No-op updates may be skipped, so success alone does not establish an operation-done NO_CHANGE result.

GCancellable parameters establish cancellation support, but these comments do not specify every cancellation checkpoint, exact error domain, response latency, or rollback boundary. The cancellation obligation targets an in-flight transaction download and makes no universal pre-cancelled-getter or exact-code claim.

Some annotations and descriptions are incomplete or inconsistent: installation/ref/instance arrays use transfer container, several instance getters omit transfer annotations, basic-auth completion mislabels its id as a webflow id, instance branch says architecture in Returns, and remote set_icon describes a homepage. Ownership obligations avoid inventing element-freeing rules or relying on these copy-and-paste mistakes.

Further documentation ambiguities include nullable previous_ids on rebase APIs, the meaning and freshness of installed_ref_get_latest_commit, and the exact unused-runtime heuristic. The requirements use nonempty previous IDs, make no remote-refresh promise for latest_commit, and do not prescribe the unspecified automatic-cleanup heuristic.

Public remote discovery documentation says only STATIC remotes are returned since 1.7 despite older remote-type prose describing LAN and USB discovery. Related-ref commits may be NULL. Instance enumeration and process tracking are inherently racy. Fixtures must control lifetime and synchronization rather than assert undocumented ordering, delays, or non-NULL values.

Signing, administrative policy, authenticators, OCI transports, sideloading, preinstallation, disk-space failures, extra-data, portal interactions, and sandbox setup each have more combinations than represented here. Public error enum membership alone does not establish a reproducible function-specific failure contract. Portal error-domain identity is included, but a portal D-Bus protocol suite is outside this library behavior inventory.

required_capabilities records coarse prerequisites for each obligation's contract and fixture, including unmapped obligations; it is not the full dependency closure or evidence of coverage. installation permits either profile, while explicit profiles require user-installation or system-installation. Object-only fixtures need no installation. local-repository means controlled repository data, not necessarily network access; bundle-files and container-images identify prepared input formats. network-observation permits asserting that no transfer occurred, controlled-transfers permits synchronizing or pacing a transfer, and fault-injection leaves the failure mechanism unspecified unless a network or filesystem tag names it. Authentication may use a controlled session-bus authenticator; system-authorization is needed when the contract exercises system authorization. sandbox-execution is required for actual launches or live sandbox fixtures, not for inspecting installed commits, permissions, or metadata. Corroborating CLI launches belong to scenario prerequisites and do not add library launch capabilities.

requirements.description: A transaction installing an available app into a fresh user installation succeeds and leaves the requested app deployed at the advertised fixture commit.

Installing an app with default dependency resolution into a fresh user installation also installs its available required runtime at the fixture runtime commit without an explicit runtime install request.
Looking up an installed user app or runtime by its full identity returns a ref whose formatted identity and commit equal the deployed fixture ref and commit.
With app A installed and B advertised, an update transaction with commit NULL succeeds and deploys B; an unchanged required runtime retains its commit.

With A installed, B advertised, and the runtime unchanged, a denied required B payload download is attempted and the update fails. The deployed app and runtime commits remain A and the original runtime commit.

An update transaction against a healthy remote advertising the already installed app and runtime commits succeeds and preserves both commits. This does not require an operation-done signal for a skipped update.

Repeating a plain transaction install of app A after its healthy remote advertises B fails with domain FLATPAK_ERROR and code FLATPAK_ERROR_ALREADY_INSTALLED. It preserves A and its unchanged runtime rather than upgrading to B.

Installing a well-formed ref absent from a healthy configured remote fails with domain FLATPAK_ERROR and code FLATPAK_ERROR_REF_NOT_FOUND. Successful installed-ref enumeration afterward returns an empty array in the initially empty user installation.
Querying a well-formed ref not installed in the user installation returns NULL with domain FLATPAK_ERROR and code FLATPAK_ERROR_NOT_INSTALLED.
A transaction uninstall request for a well-formed absent user ref fails with domain FLATPAK_ERROR and code FLATPAK_ERROR_NOT_INSTALLED and preserves the commits of an existing app and runtime.
A transaction uninstall of an installed user app succeeds and leaves that app absent from the user installation.
Enumerating installed refs in an empty user installation succeeds with a non-NULL, zero-length array, rather than representing emptiness as a failure.

After a required B payload download fails and leaves A deployed, restoring downloads and creating a new update transaction succeeds, downloads the restored B payload, deploys B, and preserves the unchanged runtime commit.
The user constructor selects the per-user installation; its path matches the configured user location, is_user is TRUE, and its ID is user.
The system constructor selects the default system-wide location, reports is_user FALSE, and reports ID default.
Constructing a configured named system installation selects that installation's path and ID rather than the default installation, and reports is_user FALSE.
System installation enumeration includes the configured reachable system installations and excludes an installation made unreachable by the fixture; it does not enumerate the per-user installation.
Constructing an installation for a supplied path with user TRUE reports that path and user profile, and its installed-ref queries address that location independently of the default user installation.

Constructing an installation for a supplied path with user FALSE reports that path and system profile, and its installed-ref queries address that location independently of the default system installation.
For a named installation with explicit display name, numeric priority, and storage type, the installation getters return those configured values.
Supported architectures are canonical names in a zero-terminated priority-ordered array whose first element equals the canonical default architecture for the fixture machine.
After another installation object changes a remote, dropping caches succeeds and a subsequent lookup on the original installation observes the changed remote configuration.

An authorized transaction in a provisioned system installation installs an available app and its required runtime in that system installation; a second user can query the installed refs with the expected commits. The caller uses a file-creation mask compatible with the documented cross-user readability prerequisite.
An authorized update transaction on system-installed A with commit NULL deploys advertised B in the selected system installation and preserves an unchanged runtime.
An authorized uninstall transaction removes the selected system-installed app, including for subsequent installed-ref queries by another user.
With the same full ref installed at different commits in user and system installations, installed-ref lookup through each installation returns that installation's commit.

Setting installation no_interaction TRUE is reflected by its getter and prevents interactive authorization dialogs during a system operation that would otherwise request authorization. Lack of authorization still produces failure rather than success.

In a fixture containing several installed apps and runtimes, installed-ref enumeration returns the complete installed set and excludes available but undeployed refs, without requiring a particular ordering.
Kind-filtered installed-ref enumeration returns exactly the installed apps for APP and exactly the installed runtimes for RUNTIME, including an empty result for a kind with no installations.
Installed-ref lookup with arch NULL and branch NULL selects the current architecture and master branch, even when a different explicit branch is also installed.
After installing different branches of an app through the direct installation API, current-app lookup identifies the last installed build and that returned installed ref reports is_current TRUE.
An installed fixture ref reports its origin remote, its actual deployment directory, and the expected installed size for that ref.
A partially installed fixture ref reports its installed subpath set; a fully installed fixture ref reports NULL rather than a partial subpath list.
Loading metadata for a deployed fixture ref returns its metadata file contents, including the fixture's declared runtime and permissions.
For an app with embedded AppStream data, loading appdata returns compressed XML matching the fixture; the name and summary getters return the fixture's localized fields under a controlled locale.

For controlled AppStream metadata, installed-ref getters return the default version, license, content-rating type, and attribute-to-value mapping. Missing optional fields return the documented NULL values.
Installed refs with explicit end-of-life reason and rebase metadata expose those values; a non-EOL fixture returns NULL for both getters.
Update enumeration includes refs with a newer remote commit or a locally downloaded but undeployed update, and excludes otherwise current refs whose dependencies are complete.
Update enumeration includes an app missing its runtime or a should-download related ref, and includes every installed app needing an update of the same shared runtime or extension.
Parsing valid full app and runtime refs preserves their kind, name, architecture, and branch; formatting each parsed ref returns its original full string.
A ref produced by parsing a valid full ref string has no commit set; get_commit returns NULL.

Parsing malformed full refs, including a missing component and an invalid kind, fails with NULL and a GError instead of producing a usable ref. No diagnostic text or undocumented exact error code is required.
Cached formatting equals the allocating formatter's full ref string and returns the same borrowed string on repeated calls for the same live immutable ref.
A ref obtained from a fixture with an explicit collection ID exposes that collection ID through the public ref getter.
Adding a new configured remote succeeds; a newly opened user installation lists and looks up that remote with its supplied name and URL.
Setting a configured remote's URL and committing it with modify_remote persists the new URL. A new installation object returns the new URL for the same remote name.

Removing an unused configured remote succeeds. A newly opened user installation excludes it from the remote list and lookup returns NULL with an error, while another configured remote remains available.

Authorized remote addition and URL modification in a named system installation persist for a second user's lookup. Removing the unused remote makes it absent there without changing the default system or per-user remote sets.

Creating a remote object does not itself configure the installation. Changing a configured remote object's URL affects that object's getter but does not change a freshly retrieved remote until changes are committed.
Adding an existing remote name with if_needed FALSE fails with FLATPAK_ERROR and ALREADY_INSTALLED and preserves its existing configuration.
Adding an existing unfiltered remote with if_needed TRUE succeeds without replacing its URL or title, even when the supplied object's URL and title differ.
Adding an existing filtered remote with if_needed TRUE using a new remote object that explicitly unsets the filter resets the persisted filter, as the documented exception to the no-change rule.
Listing several configured remotes returns them in descending priority, with earlier-added remotes before later-added remotes at equal priority.
Type-filtered remote listing includes static remotes when STATIC is requested and returns none for a USB/LAN-only request on this API version; returned remotes report STATIC.
Constructing a remote from valid flatpakrepo bytes pre-fills the supplied name, repository URL, and title without configuring an installation. Malformed flatpakrepo data returns NULL with an error.
Setting a remote title and committing it persists the supplied title across reopening the installation. Setting title NULL and committing removes the title in a fixture without a fallback title.
Explicit comment, description, and homepage edits committed to a user remote are returned unchanged by the corresponding getters after reopening the installation.
Committing explicit disabled, noenumerate, and nodeps values persists each flag independently, including toggling each back to FALSE, as verified by getters after reopening the installation.
A committed remote priority change is returned by get_prio after reopening the installation and changes the ordering relative to another remote of intervening priority.
Committing GPG verification TRUE and then FALSE on a remote without a collection ID persists each value as reported by get_gpg_verify after reopening the installation.
With a valid signed remote fixture, committed default-branch and collection-ID settings survive reopening. Explicit NULL values unset each setting and the getters then return NULL.
A valid filter pathname and explicit main ref committed to a remote are returned by their getters after reopening the installation.

Setting and committing a remote's trusted GPG key permits installation of the fixture signed by that key with verification enabled. A corresponding fixture lacking the required trusted key or signature fails instead of deploying unverified content. This obligation does not prescribe whether failure occurs during resolution or operation execution.
Listing refs by configured remote name and by its URI returns the available fixture app and runtime identities, including refs not installed locally.
Fetching a remote ref returns the remote's current commit and originating remote name even when a different commit of that ref is installed locally.

With ONLY_CACHED, remote-ref fetching and listing use cached information without network I/O. A fixture with the required cache absent fails with FLATPAK_ERROR_NOT_CACHED rather than attempting a download; stale cached data is permitted.
Remote-ref listing with ONLY_SIDELOADED includes only refs available from the fixture's sideload repositories, excluding remote-only refs.
Remote-ref listing with ALL_ARCHES includes advertised refs for fixture architectures outside the machine's primary architectures.
A remote ref backed by a populated metadata cache reports the fixture's installed size, download size, and metadata bytes. The metadata getter may return NULL when metadata is unavailable.
Remote-ref getters expose the fixture's end-of-life reason and rebased ref; a non-EOL ref returns NULL for both.
Direct metadata and size queries for a known remote ref return the fixture metadata, maximum download size, and installed size. A partially cached download may transfer fewer bytes than that maximum.

Refreshing AppStream for a remote and architecture updates the local cached content; out_changed is TRUE for changed content and FALSE for an unchanged repeat. The remote's AppStream directory getter identifies that cached content location.

Remote related-ref enumeration includes available related extensions, whereas installed related-ref enumeration includes only locally installed related refs, including an extension installed from another remote.
When the installed app and remote app require different extension branches, remote-related-refs-for-installed returns the branch appropriate to the installed version.
Related refs with different declared extension policies report whether each should be downloaded with or deleted with the main ref. Being listed does not itself imply either policy is TRUE.
Related-ref subpaths identify the fixture's partial installation set, or return NULL when all files should be installed.
For related-ref fixtures whose public should-autoprune property is TRUE or FALSE, should_autoprune returns whether the ref should be considered unused during pruning.
Opening a valid app or runtime bundle produces a bundle ref for that artifact, whose full ref, commit, and file getter match the bundle fixture and supplied file.
Bundle metadata, compressed AppStream, and installed-size getters return the embedded fixture values. Optional metadata and AppStream contents may be NULL when absent.
For a bundle containing distinct 64-pixel and 128-pixel icons, get_icon with each documented size returns the matching embedded PNG bytes.
Origin and runtime-repository URL getters return the URLs stored in the bundle; fixtures lacking those optional values return NULL.
A transaction created for an installation returns that installation through get_installation, with the same location and profile.
Installing a ref using a file:// repository URI succeeds and creates an origin remote for that installation source.
Installing a ref with explicit subpaths deploys the requested subset. NULL and an empty subpath list each request all subpaths.
An update with an explicit available commit deploys that commit even when the remote advertises a different latest commit.
Updating a partially installed locale ref with subpaths NULL preserves the current set and adds the configured languages.
For a partially installed ref, an update with either an empty subpath array or an array containing only the empty string requests all subpaths.
With no_deploy TRUE, the option getter reports TRUE and updating A downloads B without deploying B. With no_deploy later FALSE on a fresh transaction, the getter reports FALSE.
With B fully downloaded but not deployed, a no_pull transaction deploys B using only local data. The no_pull getter reflects TRUE and FALSE settings.
An uninstall request is ignored when no_deploy is enabled, and running the transaction leaves the installed ref deployed.
With runtime dependency resolution disabled, resolving an app installation does not add its absent runtime to the operations list.
With related refs disabled, resolving an app with suggested locale extensions does not add those extensions to the operations list.
Adding an installation as a dependency source allows an app to rely on its already installed required runtime without installing a second copy in the transaction's target installation.

Adding default dependency sources makes runtimes in all defined system installations available as dependencies, including a named system installation, without adding per-user installations as dependency sources.

A dynamically added local sideload repository supplies matching installation data in addition to configured sideload repositories, allowing a fixture payload to be obtained without downloading that payload from the remote.
Adding an OCI image collection using an oci: directory or oci-archive: location makes its matching images available to an OCI remote without collection-ID matching.
A transaction installs a valid signed bundle using an explicitly supplied verification key; with gpg_data NULL, it uses the embedded key when present.
Adding valid flatpakref bytes and running the transaction installs the referenced fixture artifact when the required remote additions are accepted.

Installing a container-image fixture using a supported oci:, oci-archive:, or docker: transport creates a remote for a previously uninstalled ref and reuses the existing remote when that ref was already installed.

With controlled preinstall configuration and known previously preinstalled refs, synchronizing preinstalled applications adds the required installation and removal operations and running them produces the configured set.
Adding a rebase with explicit previous application IDs installs or updates the new ref and sets up data migration from those previous IDs.
Rebase-and-uninstall installs or updates the new ref before removing the old installed ref. If the old ref was never installed, it silently omits that uninstall and still installs the new ref.
If the new ref's install or update fails in a rebase-and-uninstall transaction, the old ref's uninstall does not run and the old ref remains installed.

Enabling automatic SDK and debug installation installs the SDK for an installed or updated app and debug information for the app and its dependencies. The corresponding getters reflect each enabled setting; uninstall-only transactions do not add these installs.
An explicitly installed runtime is normally pinned against automatic removal; enabling disable_auto_pin suppresses that automatic pinning for a fresh otherwise unpinned runtime.
At ready, get_operations returns non-skipped operations in execution order, and is_empty agrees with whether that list has any operations. A resolved all-skipped transaction is empty.

Operation lookup returns the operation matching a ref and optional remote; a missing match fails with NULL and an error. If multiple remote-specific operations match and remote is NULL, lookup fails rather than choosing arbitrarily.

For controlled install, update, bundle-install, and uninstall operations, operation getters identify the requested ref, operation type, applicable remote, and bundle file where applicable. During execution get_current_operation identifies the operation being executed.
At ready for an A-to-B update with changed permissions, the operation exposes B's commit and metadata, A's old metadata, and the resolved subpath set. No subsetting is represented by NULL.

At ready, operation size getters report the ref's installed size and maximum download size excluding dependencies; both sizes are zero for uninstall operations. Actual incremental download or disk growth need not equal these figures.

A shared runtime operation reports the app operations that caused it, and a related extension reports its main operation. An explicitly requested operation with no cause reports NULL or an empty array. Traversing causes can expose skipped operations whose is_skipped getter reports TRUE.
In a multi-operation transaction, an operation completed before a later injected failure remains visible and installed after the transaction stops; the already completed operation is not rolled back.

Cancelling the GCancellable while a required update payload download is in flight causes run to finish with failure and a GError. The interrupted individual update does not replace the previously deployed app commit; previously completed operations need not be rolled back.
ready is emitted after refs are resolved to commits and required authentication is obtained; its handler can inspect the complete set of operations that will execute.
Returning FALSE from ready aborts the transaction before executing its resolved operations; returning TRUE permits their execution.

For each executed operation, new-operation arrives first with that operation and its progress object, followed by either operation-done for completion or operation-error for failure. Completed operations' done signals identify the corresponding commit when applicable.
Transaction signals are emitted in the thread executing the blocking run call, and run does not return while that transaction is still executing.

For a recoverable operation failure with an independent remaining operation, returning TRUE from operation-error permits the transaction to continue, while returning FALSE stops it. The handler receives the failing operation's GError and error details. This follows the signal documentation despite the contradictory ABORTED enum comment.

When multiple remotes supply a needed runtime, choose-remote-for-ref receives the app ref, runtime ref, and remotes in priority order. Returning an index selects that remote; returning -1 declines selection and fails resolution.
When a transaction suggests a new remote, add-new-remote supplies its reason, originating app/runtime ID, suggested name, and URL; returning TRUE adds it and returning FALSE declines the suggestion.
Processing a ref marked end-of-life emits end-of-lifed with the correct ref, reason, and optional rebase target.

end-of-lifed-with-rebase occurs before execution and supplies the remote, old ref, reason, target, and previous IDs. Its handler can add a rebase-and-uninstall and return TRUE to skip the old operation, or return FALSE to retain it.

At ready-pre-auth, the resolved operation set is available and requires_authentication identifies operations still needing token authentication. Returning FALSE aborts; TRUE allows authentication and execution to proceed.

When basic authentication is required, basic-auth-start identifies the remote and request ID. A handler returning TRUE can complete that request with valid credentials using complete_basic_auth, allowing the protected operation to proceed.

For mandatory basic authentication, returning FALSE from basic-auth-start, or accepting and completing the request with user NULL, aborts authentication and prevents the protected operation from succeeding.

An accepted webflow-start supplies the remote, browser URL, and request ID; when that webflow finishes, webflow-done supplies the same ID regardless of the authentication result. Successful mandatory authentication allows the protected operation to continue.

Calling abort_webflow with the active ID after accepting webflow-start and before webflow-done cancels that authentication request. Returning FALSE from webflow-start also aborts authentication; neither path may successfully perform a mandatory protected operation.

If resolution needs an absent but installable authenticator, install-authenticator identifies its remote and ref. Installing it from the handler permits resolution to continue; leaving the required authenticator absent causes failure.

A new transaction inherits its installation's no-interaction setting. The transaction getter reflects an explicit override, and enabling no-interaction suppresses interactive authorization dialogs for its operations.
A transaction with no parent window reports NULL. Setting an X11 or Wayland parent-window identifier makes the getter return that identifier and supplies it for authenticator UI parenting.

During a controlled transfer, changed notifications permit reading the current status, estimating flag, progress in the range 0 through 100, transferred bytes, and monotonic start time from the operation's progress object.
The transfer-rate getter reports bytes per second and returns zero during the first second while the rate is being established; a sustained controlled transfer subsequently reports a nonzero rate.
While fixture sandboxes are held alive in the current session, instance enumeration includes them and their IDs distinguish the live instances without imposing a numeric or textual ID format.
For a live controlled app sandbox, instance getters return the app ID, architecture, branch, app commit, runtime ref, and runtime commit actually used by that sandbox.
For a controlled sandbox without an application, get_app returns NULL rather than inventing an application ID.

For a synchronized live sandbox, get_pid identifies the outer babysitter and get_child_pid identifies the application process. A zero child PID is permitted briefly after launch and is not treated as a permanent result.
The instance information keyfile agrees with the fixture's /.flatpak-info inside a held-live sandbox for the app, runtime, architecture, and commit fields available there.
is_running is TRUE while a fixture sandbox is held alive and becomes FALSE after its confirmed exit, with synchronization preventing PID reuse or a lifecycle race from deciding the assertion.

Calling the library launch API for a selected installed app, architecture, branch, and available commit launches that build and returns success. The assertion must invoke libflatpak launch directly, not the CLI.
launch_full returns an instance for the application it launches; with DO_NOT_REAP, the caller can use a child watch to observe termination as documented.

A transfer-full string from format_ref remains valid after releasing its source ref and can be freed independently. Repeated allocating calls can each be freed without affecting a live ref or its cached borrowed formatter result.
The transfer-full GFile returned by get_path remains usable after the installation object is released and can be unreferenced independently.
An installed ref returned with transfer full remains usable for identity and commit inspection after its installation object is released, and the caller can release the ref independently.

Transfer-full bundle file, metadata bytes, and origin string results remain valid after releasing the bundle ref, and each result can be released independently using its documented GLib ownership convention.

A remote's transfer-full URL result survives releasing the remote. Remote-ref metadata is borrowed; taking an explicit GBytes reference while the remote ref is alive permits retaining those bytes after releasing the remote ref.

The transfer-full operations list and its operation objects, and the transfer-full installation returned by a transaction, can be retained and inspected after releasing the transaction. Borrowed related-to-ops graph elements remain safe to inspect while their parent transaction is alive; retaining an operation alone does not extend that documented graph lifetime.
A transfer-full progress status string can be retained after releasing its progress object and freed independently of later status results.

Setting languages and extra-languages to documented semicolon-separated values persists those values through get_config on a reopened installation. Unsetting a key with NULL makes get_config return NULL with G_KEY_FILE_ERROR_KEY_NOT_FOUND.

Default language and locale queries reflect explicit language configuration; the locale query preserves configured territory information. Setting languages to the empty string produces an empty language array meaning all languages.
Loading an application's overrides returns the fixture's override metadata contents for that app and selected installation.

The monitor returned for an installation emits GFileMonitor changed notifications after app or runtime installation, update, and uninstall while its main context is serviced. No exact event count or private monitored pathname is required.

The installation timestamp reports configuration modification time in Unix seconds and reflects a later installation or remote change when the fixture separates modifications by its timestamp resolution; unavailable timestamps are represented by G_MAXUINT64.

Unused-ref enumeration excludes applications, their transitively used runtimes, SDKs and extensions, and pinned runtimes. Pinned-ref enumeration includes the installed pinned fixture runtime, and an explicit architecture filters both queries.

Unused-ref queries with exclude-refs calculate usage as though those refs were absent; metadata_injection substitutes supplied metadata when calculating dependencies. These queries do not deploy, uninstall, or rewrite the installed refs.
Removing an undeployed local ref succeeds, while attempting the same API on a deployed ref returns an error and leaves it deployed. Removing an undeployed ref does not itself delete its objects.
Cleaning local refs removes undeployed refs while retaining deployed refs. Pruning afterward removes their orphaned objects while preserving data still needed by deployed refs.

Using the deprecated direct install, update, and uninstall entry points on a fixture with dependencies already satisfied installs A, returns B's installed ref after an available update, and removes the requested ref on uninstall.

A direct update_full of an already current ref returns NULL with FLATPAK_ERROR_ALREADY_INSTALLED; updating an absent ref returns NULL with FLATPAK_ERROR_NOT_INSTALLED. Both use the FLATPAK_ERROR domain.

Direct install_full with NO_DEPLOY downloads the ref without deploying it and returns NULL with FLATPAK_ERROR_ONLY_PULLED, despite completing the requested pull. The downloaded ref can subsequently be deployed with NO_PULL.
Direct install_ref_file adds a remote and returns the referenced RemoteRef without deploying the application. That returned ref has no commit set until explicitly resolved.
After direct installation, update, or uninstall with NO_TRIGGERS, calling run_triggers updates the files exported by the installed applications as documented.

A long-running AppStream refresh using the full API invokes the supplied progress callback with its user data in the caller's thread-default context; the callback is scoped to the call and reports display status, completion percentage, and estimating state.
The public Flatpak and portal error-domain functions each return a stable nonzero quark on repeated calls, and the two domains are distinct for matching their respective public error enums.
